To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
adoptive transfer of dendritic cells with tumor cells generates systemic protection against a subsequent tumor challenge in mouse models of varying immunogenecity.

DCs can prime systemic immunity against a primary tumor inoculum of a poorly immunogenic tumor, but this effect is only seen when the primary tumor is excised and a secondary tumor challenge is performed.
DCs can generate systemic antitumor responses in mouse models with undefined tumor antigens and that this effect is dependent on the immunogenicity of the tumor model.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of novel approaches to cancer immunotherapy, in particular the use of dendritic cells as antigen-presenting cells for cancer vaccines.
the generation of antitumor immunity through the use of DCs in a variety of tumor models.
the development of new immunotherapies for the treatment of cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the adoptive transfer protocol described in this paper is effective only in a mouse colorectal tumor model with a moderate degree of immunogenicity.
adoptively transferred DCs can generate systemic antitumor protection in immunogenic models of cancer.
DCs can prime systemic immunity in vivo, but this effect depends on the tumor model used and the route of DC delivery.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the use of DCs to generate systemic antitumor responses is dependent on the presence of tumor antigens capable of generating an immune response and that DCs are more effective at generating systemic immunity when the tumor is of moderate immunogenic capacity.

DCs are capable of primiing a systemic antitumor response in vivo, but only in a tumor model that is moderately immunogenic and only when the DCs are injected at the primary tumor site or in the draining lymph node.
the generation of systemic antinumor immunity by adoptivetransfer of immature DCs is dependent on the immunogenicity of the model tumor system used.
The main takeaway from our work is that

DCs can generate systemic antitumor effects in mouse models of cancer, and these effects can be enhanced by using a combination of DCs admixed either with a syngenic primary tumor inoculum or with an allogeneic primary tumor.
the use of immature DCs is effective in the induction of antitumor responses against poorly immunogenic tumors.
DCs can generate systemic antitumor effects when used as a vaccine against a primary tumor or as a therapeutic against an established tumor.
